AAA: Three phases: authentication (who are you), authorization (what may you do), accounting (what did you do)
Centralized access control for network, wireless and VPN logins
Usually delivered by a server using RADIUS; TACACS+ is the device-administration alternative
ACL: Ordered list of permit and deny rules
Attached to a resource such as a router or firewall interface, a file or a folder
Matches on things like IP address, port, protocol or user
Processed top-down: the first match wins, with an implicit deny at the end
Enforces least privilege at the network or file-system level
AD: Microsoft's directory service holding users, computers and groups
Gives centralized authentication and policy enforcement (Group Policy) for Windows domains
Works closely with LDAP for queries and Kerberos for authentication
A common attack target: Kerberoasting and pass-the-hash
AES: Symmetric block cipher, the U.S. federal encryption standard
Fast and strong: used in Wi-Fi, disk encryption and VPNs
Paired with modes such as CBC or GCM
The go-to contrast with weak legacy ciphers like DES and RC4
AES-256: AES with a 256-bit key, the strongest common AES key length
Symmetric: the same key encrypts and decrypts
Protects data at rest and in transit: full-disk encryption, VPNs, WPA2 and WPA3
Compared with AES-128: longer key, more resistance to brute force
AH: IPsec protocol giving integrity and authentication for IP packets
Adds a header containing a cryptographic hash
Does not encrypt the payload, so no confidentiality
ESP does encryption plus authentication; AH only authenticates
AI: Systems that do tasks normally needing human intelligence, such as pattern recognition and decisions
Defensive use: anomaly detection in SIEM and UEBA tools
Offensive use: automated phishing, malware creation and deepfake social engineering
AIS: U.S. government (CISA) program for sharing threat indicators in real time
Moves indicators of compromise between the public and private sectors
Automated, government-backed feed; related sharing standards are STIX and TAXII
ALE: Expected yearly money lost to one risk; a quantitative measure
SLE (loss each time) = asset value x exposure factor
Helps justify security spending against the cost of a control
AP: Device that connects wireless clients to a wired network
Broadcasts an SSID and handles Wi-Fi authentication and encryption
Rogue or misconfigured APs and evil twins are common attacks
Secure with WPA2 or WPA3 and strong authentication
API: A defined way for software components to request data or services from each other
A common integration point between cloud services and applications
Insecure APIs expose data and allow injection attacks
Controls: authentication, API keys or tokens, rate limiting
APT: Sophisticated, well-funded attacker, often nation-state sponsored
Gets in and stays undetected for a long time
Goal is espionage or data theft, not a quick smash-and-grab
Uses custom malware and patient, stealthy techniques
Told apart from hacktivists and script kiddies by persistence and resources
ARO: Estimated number of times a risk event happens per year
An input to ALE: ALE = SLE x ARO
Less than once a year is a decimal, such as 0.2 for once every five years
ARP: Resolves a known IP address to a MAC address on the local network segment
Works at the data-link layer between neighbors on a LAN
Has no authentication, so it can be spoofed or poisoned
ARP poisoning sets up on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacks
Mitigation: dynamic ARP inspection on switches
ASLR: OS technique that randomizes the memory addresses of code, stack and heap on each run
Makes memory locations hard to predict for exploits like buffer overflows
Paired with DEP as OS-level exploit mitigations
ATT&CK: MITRE knowledge base of real adversary tactics and techniques
Used to map detections, hunt threats and measure defensive coverage
Describes attacker TTPs: tactics, techniques and procedures
Not the same as the Cyber Kill Chain or the Diamond Model
AUP: Document setting the rules for acceptable use of IT systems, networks and data
Users usually must acknowledge it, often at onboarding
Violations can lead to disciplinary action
A governance document that sets expectations and consequences, alongside other policies like NDAs
AV: Methods: signature-based, heuristic and behavioral analysis
A baseline endpoint control; EDR is the more advanced successor
Struggles against zero-day and fileless malware
BASH: Common command-line shell and scripting language on Linux and Unix
Admins use it for automation; attackers use it for post-exploitation scripting
Shellshock exploited how Bash handled environment variables
The Linux counterpart to a Windows command shell
BCP: Plan to keep critical operations running during and after a disruption
A DRP is narrower: it restores IT systems
A BIA identifies the critical functions first and feeds the BCP
Backed by recovery sites: hot, warm or cold
BGP: Routing protocol that exchanges routes between autonomous systems on the internet
Decides how traffic flows between ISPs and large networks
Route hijacking or misconfiguration can redirect huge amounts of traffic
Not used inside a single LAN
BIA: Identifies and ranks an organization's critical business functions
Estimates the financial and operational impact of disruption over time
Done before planning recovery; feeds BCP and DRP
BIOS: Firmware on the motherboard that initializes hardware and loads the OS at boot
Replaced by UEFI, which adds Secure Boot
Legacy BIOS does not verify signatures during boot
So it is more exposed to boot-level malware and rootkits
BLE: Wireless personal-area technology designed for low power use
Common in IoT devices, wearables and beacons
Risks: weak or missing pairing authentication and device tracking
Can allow eavesdropping or unauthorized connection to medical devices, wearables and smart locks
BPA: Contract defining the business relationship between two organizations
Covers liability, data handling and security responsibilities
Used for shared resources or joint ventures; may include profit and loss sharing
A third-party agreement type alongside MOU, MSA and SLA
BPDU: Frames switches exchange to run the Spanning Tree Protocol
STP prevents Layer 2 loops in a switched network
Forged BPDUs can change the topology or cause denial of service
BPDU Guard disables a port that receives an unexpected BPDU, stopping rogue switches
BYOD: Employees use their own devices to reach corporate resources
Convenient and cheap, but IT has the least control over the device
Risks: data separation, device compliance, lost or stolen devices
MDM or MAM tools help enforce policy
Compare COPE (company-owned, personal use allowed) and CYOD (choose from approved devices)
C2: Channel an attacker uses to send instructions to compromised systems
Used by botnets and malware implants
Often disguised as normal traffic: DNS tunneling, beaconing over HTTPS
Spotted with behavioral or anomaly-based analysis
CA: Trusted entity that issues digital certificates
Verifies the holder's identity and binds it to a public key
The foundation of PKI trust and HTTPS, with a chain of root and intermediate CAs
A compromised CA undermines every certificate it has issued
CAB: Group of stakeholders that reviews and approves proposed IT changes
Checks risk, testing and rollback (backout) plans before a change goes live
Stops unauthorized or poorly tested changes disrupting production
CAPTCHA: Challenge-response test that tells humans from bots
Used on login and registration forms
Helps stop credential stuffing, brute force, fake account creation and scraping
A usability and security trade-off, not a strong authentication factor
CAR: Formal document written after an incident, audit finding or quality failure
Sets out the steps to fix it and stop it recurring
Gives an accountable, trackable record; a product of lessons learned
CASB: Policy enforcement point between users and cloud service providers
Delivered as software or a service
Gives visibility into shadow IT, the unsanctioned cloud apps
Enforces DLP, compliance and threat protection across SaaS applications
CBC: Block cipher mode: each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption
The first block uses an initialization vector (IV)
Chaining means identical plaintext blocks give different ciphertext
Often paired with AES; ECB, by contrast, encrypts blocks independently and leaks patterns
CCMP: AES in counter mode for confidentiality plus CBC-MAC for integrity
Replaced the weaker TKIP from the original WPA
CCPA: California privacy law protecting residents' personal information
Rights: know what is collected, request deletion, opt out of the sale of data
Applies by California residency and business revenue or data thresholds
A U.S. state counterpart to GDPR, built on opt-out rather than broad consent
CCTV: Video surveillance: cameras that monitor and record a facility
Viewed only by authorized personnel, not broadcast publicly
Used for deterrence, detection and after-the-fact investigation
A detective (and deterrent) control, not preventive: it records but does not stop an intrusion
CERT: Team of experts that responds to and coordinates computer security incidents
Often works at a national or sector level
The original at Carnegie Mellon became the model for other teams
Largely interchangeable with CSIRT, depending on the organization's naming
CFB: Block cipher mode that makes a block cipher act like a self-synchronizing stream cipher
XORs plaintext with encrypted feedback from the previous ciphertext block
Handles data that is not a multiple of the block size without padding
Unlike ECB, blocks are not encrypted independently
CHAP: Authentication protocol using a three-way handshake and a hashed challenge
The password itself is never sent over the link
Re-challenges periodically during the session, which defends against replay
Contrast with PAP, which sends credentials in cleartext
CI/CD: Practice that automates building, testing and deploying code changes often
Continuous integration merges and tests code; continuous deployment ships it
Security belongs in the pipeline (DevSecOps) so flaws are caught before production
Includes automated security testing, such as SAST and DAST, in the build
CIA: Foundational model of three security goals that every control supports
Confidentiality: only authorized parties can see the data
Integrity: data is unaltered and trustworthy
Availability: data and systems are accessible when needed
Classify controls and attacks by the leg they affect: ransomware hits availability, a breach hits confidentiality
CIDR: Method of allocating IP addresses and routing with flexible-length subnet masks
Written in slash notation, such as 10.0.0.0/24
Uses address space efficiently and allows route summarization, which shrinks routing tables
CIO: Senior executive for overall IT strategy, infrastructure and systems
Aligns IT investment with business goals
Balances security work against budget, operations and business needs
The person a CISO or security team escalates risk decisions to when they exceed the team's authority
CIRT: Designated group that detects, responds to and recovers from cybersecurity incidents
Functionally the same as a CSIRT in most organizations
The internal team that executes the incident response plan
Works through the phases: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
CIS: Nonprofit that publishes the CIS Critical Security Controls and CIS Benchmarks
Benchmarks are secure configuration baselines, also called hardening guides
Used when auditing or hardening operating systems, applications and network devices
Often used alongside STIG and NIST guidance
CMDB: Central repository of IT assets, their configurations and the relationships between them
Records configuration items and their dependencies
Helps judge the blast radius of a change or an incident
CMS: Software platform for creating, managing and publishing content, such as a website, without coding
Popular platforms are frequent attack targets
Outdated plugins, themes or core software introduce serious vulnerabilities
Defense: patch management and regular vulnerability scanning
COOP: Planning for essential functions to continue during and after a disruption
Especially associated with government and critical-function requirements
Keeps operations running during the event; disaster recovery restores systems afterward
Grouped with BCP and DRP as resilience and recovery planning
COPE: Mobile deployment model where the company owns and manages the device
Employees may also use it for personal purposes
Gives IT more control than BYOD, with some personal flexibility
Compare CYOD (choose from an approved list) and BYOD (employee-owned)
CP: Broad discipline of preparing alternative actions for when normal operations are disrupted
Umbrella over business continuity, disaster recovery and incident response
Stops the organization improvising during a crisis
The broadest term for what to do when things go wrong
CPU: The primary processor that executes instructions
Security features include virtualization extensions and secure enclaves
These support trusted execution environments and hardware-based isolation
Can be hit by side-channel exploits against processor caches
CRC: Checksum algorithm that detects accidental changes during transmission or storage
Gives no protection against deliberate tampering, unlike a cryptographic hash
Malicious tampering needs a hash such as SHA, or an HMAC
Strength order: checksum or CRC, hash, HMAC, digital signature
CRL: List published by a CA of certificates revoked before they expire
Clients check it so they do not trust a revoked certificate
OCSP is the faster alternative: real-time status for a single certificate
A CRL is downloaded periodically, so it can be stale
CSF: Voluntary framework from NIST for organizing cybersecurity activities
Core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Helps assess and improve security posture; a common language for maturity
Voluntary, unlike mandatory prescriptive standards such as PCI DSS
CSIRT: Formal team that coordinates the response to security incidents
Covers the whole lifecycle, from detection through recovery and lessons learned
The usual term for the incident response team; CIRT means the same
CSO: Senior executive for the organization's overall security strategy
May cover physical and cyber security, depending on the company
Sets security policy direction and represents security risk to leadership
Owns accountability for security risk decisions; a CISO is the cyber-specific split
CSP: Company that offers cloud services over the internet, such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud
Security is split between provider and customer: the shared responsibility model
In IaaS the customer manages more of the stack; in SaaS the CSP manages nearly everything except data and access
CSR: Message sent to a CA asking for a digital certificate
Contains the applicant's public key and identifying information
The CA validates it and returns a signed certificate
Order: generate a key pair, create the CSR, submit it to the CA, receive the signed certificate
CSRF: Web attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request
Abuses the trust a site places in the user's browser session
Fix: anti-CSRF tokens in forms, which prove the request came from the legitimate site
Different from XSS, which abuses the trust a user has in a site's content
CSU: Hardware device that connects an internal digital network to an external WAN circuit
Usually paired with a DSU; terminates the line and converts the signal
Sits at the demarcation point between customer router and carrier line, which decides who owns a fault
CTM: Counter mode (CTR) turns a block cipher into a stream cipher
Encrypts an incrementing counter and XORs the result with the plaintext
Blocks can be processed in parallel, so it is fast for high-throughput use
GCM combines counter mode with built-in authentication
CTO: Senior executive for technology direction and innovation strategy
Focused on product and engineering choices, not day-to-day IT operations
Works with the CIO and CSO so new technology does not outpace security review
Compare: the CIO runs IT operations, the CSO owns security
CVE: Standard naming system giving unique IDs to publicly known vulnerabilities
Entries include a description and references to patches or advisories
Pairs with CVSS (severity score) and NVD (the database holding the details)
CVSS: Framework that rates the severity of a vulnerability from 0 to 10
Based on factors like attack vector, complexity and impact
Used to prioritize which vulnerabilities to patch first
9.0 to 10.0 is Critical; it is a scoring system, not a database
CWE: Community catalog of common software and hardware weakness types
Examples: buffer overflow, improper input validation
Classifies the root cause behind vulnerabilities
CVE names a specific flaw in a product; CWE names the type of weakness
CYOD: Mobile deployment model where employees pick a device from a company-approved list
The organization owns or manages the device
Balances user choice with easy IT support and standard security
Compare BYOD (any personal device) and COPE (company-issued, personal use allowed)
DAC: Access control model where the resource owner decides who gets access and which permissions
Flexible, but individual users control permissions, so security is inconsistent
The default in most file systems, such as Windows NTFS
DBA: Person who manages, maintains and secures databases
Handles access permissions, performance tuning and backups
Holds powerful privileged access, so the account is a high-value target
Controls: least privilege, separation of duties, just-in-time access and session auditing
DDoS: Floods a target with traffic from many compromised devices (a botnet) at once
Overwhelms resources so legitimate users lose the service
Distributed, multi-source nature separates it from a simple DoS
Mitigation: traffic scrubbing, rate limiting and CDNs
DEP: OS feature that marks some memory regions as non-executable
Stops injected code, for example from a buffer overflow, running from the stack or heap
Core memory-exploit mitigation, paired with ASLR
DES: Legacy symmetric block cipher with a 56-bit key
Weak: it can be brute-forced with modern computing power
3DES is a variant; both are deprecated
DH: Key exchange algorithm: two parties build a shared secret over an insecure channel
The key itself is never transmitted
Not an encryption or signing algorithm
Underlies protocols like IPsec and TLS
Vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks unless combined with authentication
DHCP: Automatically assigns IP addresses and settings such as DNS servers and the default gateway
A rogue DHCP server can point clients at malicious DNS or gateways, enabling man-in-the-middle
Defense: DHCP snooping on switches blocks rogue servers
DHE: Key exchange that makes a new temporary Diffie-Hellman key pair for every session
Gives perfect forward secrecy: past sessions stay safe even if a key is later compromised
Provides forward secrecy in TLS, unlike static key exchange
DKIM: Email authentication that adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages
The receiver checks the message was not altered and came from the claimed domain
Focuses on message integrity and sender verification, with the signature in the email header
Works with SPF and DMARC to reduce spoofing and phishing
DLL: File of code and data that several programs share on Windows
DLL injection or hijacking runs malicious code inside a legitimate, trusted process
The malicious code inherits that process's permissions
Helps evade tools that look for suspicious standalone processes
DLP: Tools and policies that detect and block unauthorized sending or exposure of sensitive data
Examples: card numbers or personal data leaving by email or USB
Scans outbound email and removable media for patterns such as PII or payment card data
Enforces data-handling policy automatically; prevents exfiltration
DMARC: Email policy that says what to do when a message fails SPF or DKIM
Sends reports about authentication failures back to the domain owner
SPF and DKIM verify; DMARC enforces and reports
DMZ: Network segment between the trusted internal network and the untrusted internet
Hosts public-facing servers such as web or mail
Limits exposure of the internal network if a public server is compromised
Protected by firewalls on both sides; also called a screened subnet
DNAT: Rewrites the destination IP address of incoming packets
Forwards outside traffic to an internal server behind a firewall or router
Lets a public-facing service use a private internal address
Often used for port forwarding; standard NAT or PAT handles outbound traffic
DNS: Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses
Foundational to reaching websites, so it is a frequent attack target
Attacks: cache poisoning, hijacking, and tunneling for data exfiltration
DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to responses
DNSSEC: Adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records
Lets resolvers verify responses were not tampered with and came from the authoritative source
Protects against DNS spoofing and cache poisoning
Gives integrity and authentication, not encryption; DNS over TLS covers encrypted queries
DoS: Makes a system or service unavailable to legitimate users
Works by overwhelming it with traffic or exploiting a resource-exhaustion flaw
Comes from a single source; DDoS uses many distributed sources
Attacks the availability leg of the CIA triad
DPO: Person who oversees the organization's data privacy strategy
Ensures compliance with privacy regulations such as GDPR
Liaison between the organization, regulators and individuals about personal data
Accountable for privacy compliance; the CSO owns broader security risk
DR: Policies, tools and procedures for restoring critical IT systems and data after a disruption
Disruptions include disasters, cyberattacks and hardware failure
Guided by RTO and RPO targets
Focuses on restoring infrastructure and data; tested with tabletop exercises and failover drills
Uses recovery sites: hot, warm or cold
DRM: Access control technology that restricts how digital media and software are copied, shared or used
Enforces licensing terms through encryption and usage restrictions
Protects intellectual property after it leaves the owner's direct control
IRM applies similar ideas to enterprise documents rather than commercial media
DRP: Detailed technical steps to restore IT systems, data and infrastructure after a disruption
Example: failing over to a backup data center
An IT-focused subset of the business continuity plan
Execution is measured against RTO and RPO targets
BCP keeps the whole business running; DRP restores the technology
DSA: Public-key algorithm used only to create and verify digital signatures
Largely supplemented by RSA and ECC-based signature schemes
DSL: Delivers high-speed internet over copper telephone lines
Common for small offices and home connections
Slower and less resilient than fiber or dedicated business circuits
A single DSL line is a single point of failure for a site's availability
DSS: Security requirements from the Payment Card Industry council, known as PCI DSS
Must be followed by any organization that stores, processes or transmits credit card data
Covers network security, access control and encryption
Mandates controls such as segmenting the cardholder data environment and regular vulnerability scans
EAP: Flexible authentication framework for wireless and point-to-point connections
Commonly used with 802.1X for enterprise Wi-Fi, through a RADIUS server
ECB: Simplest block cipher mode: each block is encrypted independently with the same key
Identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks
Patterns stay visible in the ciphertext, so it is insecure for real data
The classic exam clue is a visible image pattern in encrypted output; avoid ECB
ECC: Public-key cryptography based on the mathematics of elliptic curves
Same security as RSA with much smaller keys
Efficient for smartphones, IoT sensors and other constrained devices
ECDH: Diffie-Hellman key exchange using elliptic curve cryptography
Same shared-secret negotiation with smaller keys and less computation
Popular on mobile devices and in TLS 1.3 cipher suites
Used for key exchange, not for signatures (that is ECDSA)
ECDHE: Elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman with a fresh temporary key pair for each session
Gives forward secrecy, like DHE, but with smaller and faster keys
The preferred key exchange in modern TLS
ECDSA: Digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curves
Smaller keys and faster than DSA or RSA signatures
Signing only, not key exchange (that is ECDH)
Common in TLS certificates and cryptocurrency transactions
EDR: Continuously monitors endpoint activity and detects suspicious behavior
Enables rapid investigation and response, going beyond signature-based antivirus
Gives visibility into process execution, network connections and file changes on a host
Often needed for effective incident response on endpoints
EF: Percentage of an asset's value that would be lost if a specific risk event occurred
Used with asset value to calculate SLE
A percentage, not a dollar figure by itself
EFS: Windows feature that transparently encrypts individual files and folders on NTFS
Tied to the user's account credentials
Protects data at rest from other local users
Does not help if an attacker compromises the user's own login
File-level, unlike FDE (BitLocker), which encrypts the whole disk
EMM: Broad set of tools combining mobile device, mobile application and content management
Secures and controls mobile devices and the data they access
Goes beyond device settings to cover apps and content policy
An umbrella term that includes MDM and MAM
EOL: Vendor stops selling or actively developing a product
Limited support may continue for a while
Risky: future vulnerabilities may not be patched in time
EOL is when development stops; EOS is when all support stops
EOS: Date after which the vendor gives no support, updates or security patches
Newly found vulnerabilities will never be fixed, so it is high risk
Mitigation: compensating controls, isolation or a forced upgrade
Comes after EOL, which is when active development stops
ERM: Organization-wide approach to identifying, assessing and managing risk across all business functions
Not just IT: financial, operational and reputational risk too
Aligns risk decisions with strategic objectives and risk appetite
Cybersecurity risk is one category under unified governance
ERP: Integrated platform managing core business processes: finance, HR, supply chain and inventory
One central system holding a lot of sensitive business data
A high-value target needing strong access control and monitoring
Needs RBAC and segregation of duties, such as separate create and approve rights for vendor payments
ESN: Unique identifier built into older mobile phone hardware
Tells one physical device from another on a cellular network
Used to track devices, detect fraud or block a stolen phone
A hardware identifier, separate from the phone number or account
ESP: IPsec protocol giving confidentiality through encryption, plus integrity and authentication
More widely used than AH because it encrypts
The typical choice for VPN tunnels that need confidentiality
FACL: List on a file or directory saying which users or groups can read, write or execute it
More granular than basic owner, group and everyone permissions
Lets admins give extra users specific permissions without changing ownership
Several users or groups can have different levels on the same file
FDE: Encrypts an entire drive: operating system, applications and data
Contents are unreadable without the key or credentials
Protects data at rest if a device is lost or stolen while off or locked
Example: BitLocker; it gives no protection once the system is unlocked and running
FedRAMP: U.S. program standardizing security assessment, authorization and monitoring for cloud services
Applies to cloud providers selling to federal agencies
Do once, use many times: one authorization reused across agencies
FIM: Monitors critical files and system configurations for unauthorized changes
Alerts administrators when unexpected modifications occur
Detects malware, tampering or configuration drift
A detective control, typically based on cryptographic hashes
FISMA: U.S. federal law requiring agencies and their contractors to run an information security program
NIST provides the standards and guidelines
Closely tied to the NIST Risk Management Framework, which agencies use to implement the controls
FPGA: Reconfigurable chip that can be programmed after manufacturing
Performs custom hardware functions, including cryptographic acceleration
Used in HSMs and specialized devices for high-performance cryptography
Offers flexibility fixed-function chips lack; appears in embedded and ICS security
FRR: Biometric metric: how often a legitimate user is wrongly denied access
Also called a Type I error
A high FRR frustrates real users with failed scans
Balance it against FAR (impostors wrongly accepted); CER or EER is where the two cross
FTP: Transfers files between a client and a server
Sends data and credentials in plaintext by default
Uses port 21 for control (20 for data)
Replace it with FTPS or SFTP; FTP alone offers no encryption
FTPS: FTP wrapped in TLS/SSL, encrypting authentication and data
Replaces plain FTP in security-conscious environments
Not SFTP: SFTP is a different protocol, file transfer over SSH
The similar names are a classic exam trap
GCM: Block cipher mode combining counter mode speed with a built-in authentication tag
Gives confidentiality and integrity in one pass (authenticated encryption)
Detects tampering without a separate HMAC
AES-GCM is common in modern TLS cipher suites, including TLS 1.3
GDPR: EU regulation on how organizations collect, process, store and transfer personal data of EU residents
Rights include access, correction and erasure (the right to be forgotten)
Applies to any organization handling EU residents' data, wherever it is based
Significant fines for noncompliance; breach notification timelines apply
GPG: Free, open-source implementation of the OpenPGP standard
Encrypts and digitally signs files, email and communications
Uses public-key cryptography for confidentiality and sender authenticity
Competes with S/MIME as an approach to secure email
GPO: Collection of settings in Windows Active Directory applied to users or computers
Enforces security policy: password rules, software restrictions, screen-lock timeouts
Pushes consistent configuration to many endpoints at once
A centralized policy tool, much like MDM for mobile devices
GPS: Satellite navigation giving precise location and time data to receivers
Built into phones, vehicles and asset trackers
Supports geofencing, device tracking and location-based access policies
Can be spoofed or jammed, which defeats location-based controls
GPU: Specialized processor built for graphics, now used for highly parallel computing
Attackers use GPU clusters to speed up brute-force and hash cracking far beyond a CPU
Defense: slow hashing with a work factor, such as bcrypt or Argon2
GRC: Integrated approach to align IT and security with business goals, manage risk and meet legal obligations
Governance sets the rules, risk management evaluates exposure, compliance verifies adherence
An umbrella tying together policy, risk and regulatory requirements
Often supported by dedicated GRC software platforms
GRE: Tunneling protocol that encapsulates many network-layer protocols inside point-to-point links
Often used to build VPN tunnels
Provides no encryption or authentication on its own
Paired with IPsec (GRE over IPsec) when confidentiality is needed
HA: Uses redundancy, failover and no single points of failure
Examples: clustering, load balancing and failover
Supports the availability leg of the CIA triad and business continuity
HDD: Storage that uses spinning magnetic platters
Must be sanitized before disposal so the data cannot be recovered
Methods: degaussing, multi-pass wiping or physical destruction
HIDS: Monitors one host's system logs, file integrity and activity for signs of compromise
Does not watch network traffic; NIDS does
Catches threats that only show once they run on the endpoint, even ones hidden from network sensors by encryption
Detects and alerts only; HIPS also blocks
HIPAA: U.S. federal law protecting sensitive patient health information (PHI)
Applies to healthcare providers, insurers and their business associates
Requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards
Includes breach notification requirements, distinct from general privacy laws like GDPR
HIPS: Monitors one host and automatically blocks malicious activity
Example: stopping a suspicious process or changes to protected files
Prevents in real time, unlike HIDS, which only alerts
Same detect vs prevent split as NIDS and NIPS on the network
HMAC: Combines a cryptographic hash with a secret key
Verifies both integrity and authenticity of a message
Only someone with the shared key can produce a valid code
A plain hash such as SHA gives integrity only, with no authentication
HOTP: One-time password built from an HMAC and a counter that increments with each use
Counter-based: the code stays valid until it is used
TOTP is time-based and expires after a short window
Both are common token mechanisms for MFA
HSM: Dedicated, tamper-resistant physical device that generates, stores and manages cryptographic keys
Performs cryptographic operations without exposing the keys to the host
Stronger key protection than software key storage
Used in PKI and high-security environments that need FIPS-validated hardware
HTML: Standard markup language that structures and displays web page content
User input reflected as HTML without sanitizing is the root cause of cross-site scripting
Unsanitized input can run as HTML or JavaScript in the victim's browser
HTTP: Foundational protocol for transferring web content between clients and servers
Sends data in plaintext, so it can be eavesdropped on and tampered with
HTTPS adds TLS encryption; plain HTTP traffic is a finding in a security assessment
HTTPS: Protects the confidentiality and integrity of web traffic between browser and server
Lets the client verify the server's identity through its digital certificate
Uses port 443; the padlock does not guarantee the site's content is trustworthy
HVAC: Regulates temperature and humidity, which is critical in data centers
Keeps servers within safe environmental limits, protecting availability
Increasingly networked and controlled by ICS or SCADA components
Network-connected HVAC expands the attack surface
IaaS: Cloud model where the provider supplies virtualized servers, storage and networking
Customer manages the operating system, applications and data
Most control, and the most security responsibility, compared with PaaS and SaaS
Customer handles OS patching and application security; the provider secures the physical infrastructure
IaC: Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files
Security benefit: configurations are consistent and auditable
Risk: one flawed template spreads vulnerabilities across many systems at once
IAM: Policies, processes and technologies for managing digital identities and controlling their access
Covers provisioning, authentication, authorization and deprovisioning across the identity lifecycle
The umbrella over AAA, SSO, MFA and RBAC
ICMP: Used by network devices to send diagnostic and error messages
The protocol behind ping and traceroute
Abused for reconnaissance, such as ping sweeps
Abused for DoS: ping of death and smurf attacks
Firewalls often rate-limit or block it
ICS: Systems that control industrial processes and critical infrastructure, such as power grids, water treatment and manufacturing
Often run legacy, unpatched software that was not built with network security in mind
Hard to patch while live, so a high-value, high-risk target
Defense: segmentation that isolates OT from IT networks
IDEA: Symmetric block cipher, a patented alternative to DES
Used in early versions of PGP for email encryption
Superseded by AES; a legacy cipher, not the current recommended standard
IDF: Smaller wiring closet, typically one per floor, linking local cabling back to the main distribution frame
Needs physical security: locked and access-controlled
Physical access to wiring allows eavesdropping or tampering and bypasses many logical controls
IdP: Service that creates, maintains and authenticates digital identities
Asserts the user's identity to other applications (service providers)
Users do not need separate credentials for each application
Core of federation and SSO (SAML, OIDC): the relying party trusts the IdP's assertion or token
IDS: Monitors network or host activity for malicious behavior or policy violations
Generates alerts but does not block traffic
A passive, detective control, not a preventive one
Contrast IPS, which detects and actively blocks
IEEE: Professional standards organization behind many networking and security standards
The 802 family: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 wireless LANs, 802.1X port-based network access control
Exam questions often cite the standard number rather than spelling out IEEE
IKE: Protocol that sets up a secure, authenticated channel and negotiates keys for an IPsec VPN
Handles key management so AH and ESP use fresh, agreed keys for each session
Runs first, before AH or ESP can protect the actual traffic
IM: Unmonitored or unsanctioned IM creates data loss and malware delivery risks
Messages and attached files can bypass email security controls
A social engineering vector that often sits outside email monitoring and DLP
IMAP: Email retrieval protocol that keeps messages synchronized on a central server
Allows access from several devices at once
Unencrypted IMAP exposes credentials and content, so use TLS
SMTP sends mail; POP3 does simple download-and-delete retrieval
IoC: Forensic evidence suggesting a breach or malicious activity
Examples: a malicious IP address, file hash, domain name or registry key
The artifacts analysts search for to detect known malicious activity
Shared through threat intelligence feeds, often in STIX format
IoT: Internet-connected physical devices such as smart cameras, thermostats and sensors
Limited processing power and minimal built-in security
Often ship with default credentials and are rarely patched
Popular botnet targets, for example Mirai DDoS botnets
IP: Network-layer protocol responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks
Firewalls, VPNs, ACLs and NAT all work on or around IP addressing
Know the difference between public and private address ranges
IPS: Monitors network traffic and automatically blocks malicious activity in real time
Sits inline so it can drop malicious packets before they arrive
Active, unlike IDS, which is passive and alerts only
Must be placed inline to intercept and stop traffic
IPSec: Suite of protocols giving authentication and encryption for IP packets
Commonly used for VPN tunnels between sites or for remote users
Includes AH and ESP, with IKE for key management
Tunnel mode encrypts the whole original packet; transport mode encrypts only the payload
IPv4: Fourth version of IP: 32-bit addresses written as four decimal octets
Limited address space led to widespread use of NAT
Address exhaustion drove the move to IPv6
IPv6: A vastly larger address space ends address exhaustion
Built-in autoconfiguration and simpler header processing
Designed partly to remove the need for NAT
Watch for IPv6 traffic bypassing firewall rules written only for IPv4
IR: Organized approach to detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from a security incident
Guided by a predefined incident response plan for a consistent reaction under pressure
Phases in order: preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
IRC: Widely abused as a command-and-control channel for botnets
Unexpected outbound IRC traffic from an internal host is a classic indicator of compromise
IRM: Data protection technology that embeds persistent access controls in documents and emails
Can restrict printing, copying or forwarding
Protection travels with the file, even outside the organization's network
Protects internal business documents; DRM protects commercial media
IRP: Documented procedures and responsibilities guiding the response to a security incident
Defines roles, communication plans and the steps for each phase
The written document; incident response (IR) is the process it guides
Should be tested regularly with tabletop exercises
ISO: International body that publishes voluntary standards
ISO 27001 covers information security management systems
Organizations get certified to show a mature, internationally recognized security program
A standard you can be audited and certified against
ISP: Company that gives organizations and individuals access to the internet
Delivers the physical or wireless circuit to the wider internet
A single ISP is a single point of failure
Resilience: two ISPs over physically diverse paths, so one fiber cut does not take both down
ISSO: Person responsible for one information system or program's security controls and compliance
Ensures the system meets organizational and regulatory requirements
Common in government and federal contracting, following NIST RMF
Accountable for that system's day-to-day security compliance posture
ITAM: Tracking and managing hardware and software assets across their lifecycle, from purchase to disposal
Keeps accurate inventories and controls cost
You cannot protect or patch what you do not know you have
ITIL: Framework of best practices for IT service management
Defines structured processes for incident, change and problem management and service delivery
Aligns IT services with business needs
A process framework for running IT operations, not a technical security control
IV: Random or pseudo-random value used with a key when encrypting
Ensures the same plaintext encrypted twice gives different ciphertext
Must be unique, and often unpredictable, for every encryption operation
Reused or predictable IVs broke WEP
KDC: Trusted third-party service at the center of Kerberos
Issues session tickets and temporary keys to clients and servers
Lets parties authenticate without directly sharing long-term secrets
Issues a ticket-granting ticket (TGT), which is then used to request service tickets
KEK: Key used only to encrypt other keys, such as a data encryption key
Key wrapping: the data key is never stored or sent in the clear
Forms a key hierarchy, often inside a KMS or HSM
KMS: Centralized system to generate, store, distribute, rotate and revoke cryptographic keys
Manages keys across their whole lifecycle
Cloud providers offer KMS so customers can manage keys for cloud-stored data
Customers do not have to build their own key infrastructure
L2TP: Tunneling protocol used to create VPN connections
Provides no encryption on its own
Almost always paired with IPsec: L2TP/IPsec
An unencrypted tunneling protocol plus a separate security protocol points to L2TP/IPsec
LAN: Network confined to a small area such as an office building or campus
Devices share resources and communicate at high speed
Scope in order: LAN, then MAN, then WAN
Segment with VLANs and NAC to limit lateral movement if one part is compromised
LDAP: Protocol for querying and modifying directory services
Example: looking up user and group information in Active Directory
Plaintext on port 389, so queries and credentials are exposed unless secured
LDAPS on port 636 is the encrypted version
LDAPS: Protects directory queries and credentials from eavesdropping
Preferred over plaintext LDAP in production
LEAP: Cisco's proprietary early EAP method for Wi-Fi
Weak: its MS-CHAP-based authentication is open to offline dictionary attacks
Deprecated and insecure; finding it in a wireless audit is a weakness
Replaced by stronger EAP methods such as PEAP and EAP-TLS
MaaS: Cloud service where a third party monitors your infrastructure, applications or security events
Works through agents or log forwarding to the provider's platform
Outsources continuous monitoring without building your own monitoring team
Brings third-party risk management considerations, like other XaaS models
MAC: Mandatory Access Control: a central authority assigns security labels to users and resources
Access is granted only when labels match, under strict system-enforced policy
Users cannot override or delegate permissions, unlike DAC
Common in military and government systems, for example SELinux
Also means Media Access Control (hardware address) and Message Authentication Code (integrity check); context decides
MAM: Manages and secures specific apps and their data on a mobile device
Does not control the entire device
Suits BYOD: corporate apps protected, personal apps and data untouched
MDM controls the whole device; MAM works at the app level
MAN: Network that spans a city or metropolitan region
Often connects several campus or branch LANs
Sits between a LAN (building-sized) and a WAN (national or global)
MBR: First sector of a drive, holding the bootloader and partition table
Runs before the operating system loads
Malware here is a bootkit, very hard to detect and remove
UEFI Secure Boot is designed to prevent this persistence technique
MD5: Known collision vulnerabilities make it unsuitable for digital signatures and other security uses
Still seen for non-security checks, such as spotting accidental file corruption
MDF: Primary wiring point of a building, where carrier lines and internal cabling meet
The central hub that all the building's IDFs connect back to
Kept in a secured central equipment room
MDF and IDF both need strong physical security against tampering and eavesdropping
MDM: Software that lets IT enforce policies, configure settings and remotely wipe mobile devices
Central, device-level control across the fleet
Enforces encryption, passcodes and remote wipe
Works across BYOD, COPE and CYOD deployments
MDR: Outsourced security service: a provider monitors your environment around the clock
Combines technology and human analysts to detect, investigate and respond to threats
A service model (people plus technology), not just a product like EDR or NDR
Fits organizations without in-house 24/7 SOC staff
MFA: Requires two or more independent types of credential before granting access
Factors: something you know, something you have, something you are
Stays safer even if one factor, like a password, is stolen
Factors must come from different categories: two passwords is still single-factor
MFD: Office device combining printing, scanning, copying and faxing in one networked unit
Runs an embedded OS, stores scanned documents and sits on the network
An overlooked attack surface, often unpatched and unmonitored
Cached copies of documents on its drive can leak sensitive data
MFP: Same idea as an MFD: one device that prints, scans, copies and sometimes faxes
The two terms are used interchangeably
Needs firmware updates, strong admin credentials and restricted network access
Often missed in patch management and asset inventories
MITM: Attacker secretly intercepts, and may alter, communication between two parties
Positioning methods: ARP poisoning, rogue access points (evil twin), SSL stripping
Defenses: mutual authentication and certificate validation
ML: Subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data to predict or decide, without being programmed for every case
Powers anomaly detection such as UEBA and modern antivirus or EDR engines
Can itself be tricked or attacked, for example by poisoning training data
MMS: Mobile standard for messages with images, video or audio, extending text-only SMS
Can carry phishing: smishing, with malicious links or attachments
Arrives outside email filtering and email-only awareness training
MOA: Formal document between parties setting out an agreed course of action, responsibilities and resources
More formal and detailed than an MOU
Grouped with MOU, SLA and BPA as agreement types
MOU: Informal, usually non-binding document expressing shared intent or understanding
Without the legal weight of a formal contract
Often written before a formal agreement is drafted
Less formal than an MOA or BPA
MPLS: Carrier WAN technology that forwards traffic using short labels instead of full routing lookups at every hop
Connects branch offices with predictable performance
A private, carrier-managed alternative to sending site-to-site traffic over the public internet
SD-WAN is the more modern, flexible alternative
MSA: Contract setting general terms that govern future agreements or transactions between two parties
Specific project details go in a related SOW
Each new engagement avoids a full contract renegotiation
MSCHAP: Microsoft's extension of CHAP, adding mutual authentication and stronger password hashing
MSCHAPv2 still has known cryptographic weaknesses
Usually run inside a PEAP tunnel (PEAP-MSCHAPv2) for protection
MSP: Third party that remotely manages a customer's IT infrastructure, such as networks or help desk
Needs privileged access to client environments, which is a supply-chain risk
Manages general IT; an MSSP manages security specifically
MSSP: Third-party provider delivering outsourced security monitoring and management
Examples: SOC-as-a-service, SIEM monitoring, vulnerability management
Gives 24/7 threat monitoring to organizations without in-house security staff
MTBF: Average expected time between failures of a repairable system
Reliability metric used to estimate hardware dependability and plan maintenance
A higher MTBF means a more reliable component
Pairs with MTTR: MTBF is reliability, MTTR is how fast you fix it
MTTF: Average expected time until a non-repairable component fails and must be replaced
MTBF applies to repairable systems, MTTF to ones that are replaced
MTTR is how long a repair takes
MTTR: Average time to diagnose, fix and restore a failed system to normal operation
Organizations aim to minimize it to limit downtime
Discussed with MTBF (how often failures happen) and RTO (target recovery time)
MTU: Largest packet size that can cross a network link without fragmentation
Fragmentation-based attacks try to evade inspection by security devices
Comes up in network performance troubleshooting
NAC: Checks a device's compliance (updated antivirus, patches) before granting network access
Can restrict or quarantine non-compliant devices
Posture assessment: failing devices go to a quarantine VLAN until remediated
NAT: Translates private internal IP addresses to a public address and back as traffic crosses a boundary
Lets many internal devices share one public address
Hides internal addressing from outside view
Not a firewall: it does not filter traffic by security policy
NDA: Legal contract obliging the signers to keep specified information confidential
Signed by employees, contractors and business partners who see sensitive data
Protects confidentiality, not service terms or performance
Sits with MOU and BPA as an agreement type
NDR: Uses behavioral analytics and machine learning on network traffic to find anomalous or malicious activity
Catches things like lateral movement and command-and-control traffic
Analyzes network traffic, not endpoint telemetry; sits beside EDR and XDR
NetFlow: Cisco protocol that collects metadata about IP traffic flows
Records source and destination addresses, ports and byte counts, not payloads
Shows who talked to whom and how much, for anomaly detection at scale
Feeds SIEM or NDR tools without the storage cost of full packet capture
NFC: Short-range wireless technology for exchanging data between devices very close together
Used for contactless payments and access badges
Short range limits, but does not remove, interception and relay attack risk
NGFW: Firewall that adds deeper inspection to port and protocol filtering
Application-aware inspection, integrated IPS and identity-based rules
Blocks threats by application behavior, not only IP address and port
Combines firewall, IPS and application control in one appliance
Seen as the modern replacement for a traditional stateful firewall alone
NIC: Hardware (a card or chip) that connects a computer to a network
Provides physical and data link layer functions
Each has a unique MAC address
Where port security and 802.1X access control are enforced when a device connects
NIDS: Monitors traffic across a whole network segment
Analyzes copies of traffic and alerts, without blocking it
Deployed at a chokepoint through a SPAN port or network tap
Sees patterns across many hosts; a host-based IDS watches one system
NIPS: Monitors network traffic in real time and blocks malicious traffic inline
Sits directly in the traffic path, so it can stop an attack before it reaches the target
A misconfiguration can disrupt legitimate traffic
NIDS watches a copy through a tap or mirror port and only alerts
NIST: U.S. government agency that publishes cybersecurity frameworks, guidelines and standards
Examples: Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), Risk Management Framework (RMF), the SP 800 series
Many compliance programs and best practices point back to NIST publications
NOC: Central location where staff monitor network infrastructure performance and availability around the clock
Focuses on network performance and uptime
A SOC focuses on security events
The two often collaborate, sharing tools and escalating issues to each other
NTFS: Default file system on modern Windows
Fine-grained file and folder permissions, encryption (EFS) and detailed audit logging
Enforces discretionary access control on files and folders
FAT32 has no native permissions or encryption
NTLM: Legacy Microsoft authentication protocol using challenge-response
Largely replaced by Kerberos in Active Directory
Vulnerable to relay and pass-the-hash attacks
Guidance is to disable it where possible
NTP: Synchronizes clocks across computers and network devices
Log correlation, certificate validity and time-limited tickets all depend on matching clocks
Without it, timestamps from different systems cannot be reliably correlated in an investigation
Ticket-based authentication can fail if clock drift exceeds its tolerance
NVD: U.S. government repository of enriched data on publicly disclosed CVE entries
Adds analysis, CVSS severity scores and affected product lists
Used to research vulnerabilities and prioritize patching
CVE names the flaw, CVSS scores it, NVD holds the details
OAUTH: Lets a user give a third-party app limited access to their resources without sharing a password
Grants access tokens for resource access; it does not verify identity by itself
Authorization, not authentication; OIDC adds identity on top
OCSP: Protocol for checking in real time whether a certificate has been revoked
Asks about a single certificate instead of downloading a whole CRL
Speeds up certificate validation during TLS handshakes
OCSP stapling lets the web server supply the signed response itself
OID: Globally unique, hierarchical string of numbers that names an object, policy or attribute type
Most often seen identifying extensions and policies in X.509 certificates
Lets systems unambiguously reference a standard or field
Just an identifier, not an encryption algorithm
OIDC: Identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0
Lets an application verify a user's identity and get basic profile information through an identity provider
Adds an ID token to OAuth's access token
Handles authentication (who you are); OAuth handles authorization (what you can access)
Common for single sign-on web logins
OS: Foundational software that manages hardware and runs all other applications
Where patching, hardening and privilege management happen
An outdated or end-of-life OS is a recurring exam theme for unmitigated vulnerability risk
OSI: Conceptual seven-layer model of how network communication functions are organized
Layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Used to place protocols, devices and attacks
Switches and VLANs at Layer 2, routers and IP at Layer 3, firewalls at Layers 3 to 4, web application attacks at Layer 7
OSINT: Information gathered from public sources: social media, websites, public records
Used in reconnaissance by penetration testers and threat actors
Involves no direct interaction with the target's systems
Listed as a threat intelligence source
OSPF: Calculates the shortest paths between routers inside a network
Widely used in large enterprise and service-provider networks
Enable route authentication to stop route injection or spoofing through a rogue router
OT: Hardware and software that monitors and controls physical devices and industrial processes, such as SCADA
Often prioritizes availability and safety over confidentiality
Preferred controls: network segmentation and monitoring rather than disruptive patching
OTA: Wireless delivery of software, firmware or configuration updates to a device, with no cable
Common for smartphones, IoT devices and connected vehicles
Must be secured with code signing and encrypted delivery
An insecure channel lets an attacker push malicious firmware to thousands of devices at once
OVAL: Standardized XML-based language for describing system configuration, vulnerabilities and compliance checks
Lets automated tools assess machine state consistently
Describes the checks; it does not perform the scan itself
OWASP: Nonprofit community producing free resources on web application security
Best known for the OWASP Top 10, a regularly updated list of the most critical web application risks
Examples on the list: injection and broken access control
Authoritative source for web app risk categories, testing guides and secure coding standards
P12: Password-protected archive (also called PFX) bundling a private key with its certificate and chain
Used to move a certificate and its private key together, for example to a new server
Contains the private key, so it needs a strong password and careful handling
Unlike a public-only certificate file such as .cer
P2P: Devices communicate and share resources directly instead of through a central server
Seen in file sharing and some blockchain and cryptocurrency networks
A common vector for malware distribution
Misconfigured sharing can leak sensitive files from a corporate machine
Restrict with policy: an AUP or application allow-listing
PaaS: Cloud model giving a managed runtime: operating system, middleware and development tools
Developers build and deploy apps without managing the infrastructure
Provider manages the OS and runtime; the customer owns the application code and data
Sits between IaaS and SaaS on the shared responsibility model
PAC: Small script that tells a browser which proxy server to use for a given URL
Gives automatic, centralized control of how web traffic is routed
Forces browsers through inspection proxies or content filters, such as a secure web gateway
Distributed automatically rather than configured by hand on each device
PAM: Privileged Access Management: tools and policies to control, monitor and audit accounts with elevated permissions
Reduces the attack surface of standing privileged access
Techniques: credential vaulting, just-in-time elevation, session recording
Minimizes the time and scope of elevated privileges rather than eliminating them
Also means Pluggable Authentication Modules, a Linux authentication framework
PAP: Legacy authentication protocol for point-to-point links
Sends usernames and passwords in plaintext
No encryption or protection against eavesdropping
Replaced by CHAP and EAP; passwords sent unencrypted during PPP authentication means PAP
PAT: NAT variant that maps many internal private addresses to one public address using port numbers
Conserves public IPv4 addresses and hides the internal topology
Static NAT (and DNAT) maps one-to-one instead
PBKDF2: Key derivation function that hashes a password with a random salt thousands or millions of times
Deliberately slow, to resist brute-force and rainbow table attacks
A key-stretching algorithm, like bcrypt and Argon2
Used to store password hashes and to derive encryption keys from passphrases
Salt plus a configurable iteration count raises the attacker's cost
PBX: Private telephone switching system that routes calls inside an organization
Connects internal extensions to outside phone lines
Attacks: toll fraud, eavesdropping and voicemail hacking
Default credentials and remote administration are common vectors, and it can be a pivot into the corporate network
PCAP: File format and method for recording the full contents of network traffic on an interface
Essential for deep forensic analysis and troubleshooting
Costly to store at scale; NetFlow keeps only metadata
Tools like Wireshark read PCAP files
PCI: Refers to PCI DSS: security requirements for organizations handling credit card data
Non-compliance can mean fines, higher fees or loss of card processing privileges
An industry standard rather than a government law; applies to any size of organization
PCI DSS: Contractual security standard created by the major card brands
Requirements include network segmentation, encryption, access control and regular testing
Applies to any organization that stores, processes or transmits card data, regardless of size
Expect it in e-commerce and retail scenarios
PDU: Device that distributes electrical power from one source to many pieces of equipment in a rack or data center
Often has remote monitoring and outlet-level switching
Part of availability planning alongside UPS systems and backup generators
Dual PDUs on separate circuits stop one power failure taking down a whole rack
PEAP: EAP version that wraps the authentication exchange in an encrypted TLS tunnel
Credentials are only sent after the tunnel is up, so they are not exposed in plaintext over the air
Used for wireless authentication in WPA2 and WPA3 Enterprise, with 802.1X
Like HTTPS protecting HTTP: tunnel first, then authenticate
PED: Personally owned portable device, such as a smartphone, tablet or smartwatch
Risks in secure facilities: unauthorized photos, audio recording, data exfiltration and malware from unmanaged devices
Physical security control: restrict PEDs in sensitive areas like data centers or SCIFs
Often enforced alongside clean desk and visitor logging policies
PEM: Base64 ASCII text format for storing X.509 certificates, private keys and certificate chains
Delimited by header and footer lines such as BEGIN CERTIFICATE
Readable as plain text, unlike binary formats such as DER or PKCS#12
A .pem file can hold a certificate, a private key, or both
PFS: Property of key exchange: every session uses a unique, temporary key
Session keys are not derived from a long-term private key
If the server's private key is stolen later, captured past sessions still cannot be decrypted
Comes from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE), preferred over static RSA key exchange
PGP: Encryption application for email and files giving confidentiality, integrity and authentication
Trust model: decentralized web of trust
S/MIME is the alternative, with hierarchical CA-based trust
PHI: Individually identifiable health information, such as medical records, diagnoses or treatment history
Created, received or maintained by a healthcare provider
Protected under HIPAA, with specific breach reporting and penalty rules
Distinct from PII; a hospital or clinic breach signals PHI obligations
PII: Data that identifies a specific individual on its own or combined with other information
Examples: name, Social Security number, email address
A core driver of data classification, privacy law and DLP programs
Tested alongside PHI; expect questions about labeling, handling or breaches of customer PII
PIV: Government-issued smart card that cryptographically proves an employee's or contractor's identity
Used for physical building access and logical access to computer systems
Combines a certificate-holding chip with a PIN
Gives MFA in one credential: something you have plus something you know; CAC is the paired example
PKCS: Numbered specifications (PKCS#1 to PKCS#15) published by RSA Security
Define standard formats and procedures for public-key cryptography
PKCS#12 bundles a certificate with its private key (.p12 or .pfx)
Promote interoperability between cryptographic software and hardware
PKI: Framework of policies, roles, hardware and software to create, manage, distribute, store and revoke certificates and public keys
Underpins trust for TLS, email encryption and code signing
Components: CAs, RAs, CRLs, OCSP, certificate chains of trust
Scenarios cover certificate issuance, revocation and trust validation
POP: Downloads messages to a single client, typically deleting them from the server
Port 110, or 995 for POP3S; no native encryption
Unlike IMAP, it does not keep mail synchronized across devices
POTS: No encryption, authentication or modern signaling features
A forgotten line, for a fax machine or alarm dialer, is a legacy path into a facility
It bypasses network security monitoring entirely
PPP: Data link layer protocol that sets up a direct connection between two nodes
Used for dial-up, DSL and some WAN links
Supports authentication with PAP and CHAP
PAP sends credentials in clear text; CHAP uses challenge-response
PPTP is different: it tunnels PPP over an IP network for VPNs
PPTP: Early VPN tunneling protocol that wraps PPP packets for transport across an IP network
Now insecure: weaknesses in MS-CHAPv2 authentication and encryption
Deprecated; replace with a stronger option such as an IPsec-based VPN
PSK: Secret shared in advance between two parties, to authenticate or derive encryption keys
Seen in WPA2 or WPA3 Personal Wi-Fi and some site-to-site VPNs
Everyone uses the same key, so it scales poorly
Cannot revoke one user without changing the key for everyone
WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X with individual RADIUS credentials instead
PTZ: Security camera that can be remotely panned, tilted and zoomed
Actively tracks activity across a wide area instead of a single fixed view
Lets a smaller security staff cover more ground
A detective physical control, often combined with motion detection to track movement
PUP: Software bundled with a legitimate installer, installed with minimal or deceptive consent
Often shows intrusive ads, changes browser settings or tracks activity
Classify an unwanted toolbar or bundled adware as a PUP, not a virus or trojan
RA: Recovery Agent: a trusted role holding special keys that can recover encrypted data if the original key is lost
Key-escrow scenario: for example, decrypting EFS-protected files
Also means Registration Authority, the PKI component that verifies identity before a CA issues a certificate
A Registration Authority offloads identity checking from the CA; context decides which meaning applies
RACE: European research program funding advanced communications and cryptography research
Its work led to the RIPEMD family of hash functions
On the exam it mainly explains where RIPEMD came from
RAD: Development methodology built on quick iterative prototyping and continuous user feedback
Delivers working software faster than traditional waterfall
Less upfront planning than a rigid SDLC
Security must keep pace, for example with automated scanning in CI/CD
RADIUS: Centralized client/server protocol giving AAA for users connecting to a network
Uses UDP and a shared secret between client and server
Encrypts only the password field, unlike protocols that encrypt the whole payload
RAID: Combines several physical disks into one logical unit
Gives speed, fault tolerance, or both, depending on the level
RAID 0 striping: fast, no redundancy. RAID 1 mirroring: survives one disk failure
RAID 5 and 6 stripe with parity (one and two disk failures survived); RAID 10 is mirrored stripes
Supports availability but is not a backup: it will not save you from deletion or ransomware
RAS: Server or service giving remote users a secure entry point into the internal network
Historically over dial-up, now typically over VPN
Centralizes authentication and policy enforcement for remote connections
RAT: Malware giving an attacker covert remote control of an infected system
Enables keylogging, file exfiltration and webcam or microphone access
Arrives disguised as legitimate software or through phishing attachments
Told apart from legitimate remote access software by its covert, unauthorized nature
RBAC: Role-Based Access Control: permissions are granted by a user's assigned role, not to each individual
Adding or removing a role adjusts access automatically, so it scales well
Ties permissions to job function, making onboarding, offboarding and audits consistent
Also means Rule-based Access Control: administrator-defined if-then rules
RC4: Once widely used in WEP and early SSL/TLS
Cryptographically broken because of biases in its keystream
RCA: Structured process after an incident to find the underlying cause, not just the symptoms
Belongs to the lessons-learned phase of incident response
Answers why it happened, to drive process or control improvements
RCE: Vulnerability that lets an attacker run arbitrary code on a target from a remote location
Can lead to complete system compromise
The highest-severity outcome, often scored Critical in CVSS
Typical causes: unpatched software, deserialization flaws and buffer overflows
RDP: Microsoft protocol for viewing and controlling another Windows computer's full desktop over a network
A frequent target for brute force and credential stuffing when exposed to the internet
A common path to ransomware; mitigate with a VPN or RAS gateway, MFA and account lockout
RF: Electromagnetic spectrum range used for wireless communication: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID
Concerns: jamming, eavesdropping and unauthorized signal injection
RF interference can act as a denial-of-service attack on wireless availability
RF signal analysis is part of a wireless site survey
RFC: Formal document from the IETF that defines internet standards, protocols and best practices
Examples: the documents defining IP or RADIUS
The authoritative specification vendors implement for interoperability
No need to memorize numbers; know RFCs are the mechanism behind internet protocols
RFID: Wireless technology that uses radio waves to identify and track tags on objects, badges or inventory
Needs no line of sight or contact
Commonly used for building access badges
Unencrypted or poorly secured tags can be cloned or skimmed with a cheap reader
RIPEMD: Family of cryptographic hash functions; RIPEMD-160 is the most widely used
Designed as an alternative to MD5 and SHA
Produces a fixed-length digest to verify integrity, not an encryption algorithm
Less common than SHA-2 today, but seen in some cryptocurrency and legacy systems
Originated from the RACE research program
RMF: NIST-defined process for building security and risk management into a system's lifecycle
Steps: categorize, select, implement, assess, authorize, monitor
Widely mandated for U.S. federal information systems
Cyclical and ongoing, with continuous monitoring, not a one-time checklist
ROI: Financial metric comparing the benefit of an investment to its cost, as a ratio or percentage
In security, weighs a safeguard's cost against the reduction in expected loss
Used with ALE and ARO to judge whether a control is cost-effective
RPO: Maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time, after a disruption
How far back in time backups must reach
Drives how frequently backups are taken
RPO is data loss tolerance; RTO is downtime tolerance
RSA: Widely used asymmetric algorithm based on the difficulty of factoring large primes
Used for key exchange, digital signatures and certificate encryption
Underpins much of PKI and TLS key exchange
ECC is the faster, smaller-key alternative with equivalent security
RTBH: Network defense technique using BGP to send traffic for a target IP into a null route
Drops traffic at the network edge before it eats bandwidth or reaches the destination
Used by ISPs and large networks to mitigate volumetric DDoS
Works at the routing layer by discarding traffic for a black-holed address, often coordinated with an upstream ISP
RTO: Maximum acceptable time a system or process can be down before causing unacceptable harm
Drives the design and cost of disaster recovery
A shorter RTO typically needs more expensive high-availability solutions
RTO is how long you can be down; RPO is how much data you can lose
RTOS: Operating system that processes inputs and runs tasks within strict, guaranteed time limits
Used in embedded systems, industrial controllers and IoT devices where predictable timing is critical to safety
Often cannot be patched like a general-purpose OS without risking timing failures
Compensating controls such as network segmentation are essential
RTP: Delivers audio and video over IP networks in real time
The media transport underneath VoIP and video conferencing
No encryption of its own, so calls can be eavesdropped
Pair it with SRTP when voice or video confidentiality is needed
S/MIME: Standard for public-key encryption and digital signing of email
Relies on certificates from a trusted CA to confirm sender identity and encrypt content
Built into enterprise email clients such as Outlook
Hierarchical CA trust suits managed enterprises; PGP uses a web of trust instead
SaaS: Cloud model where the provider hosts and manages a complete application, usually on subscription
No infrastructure to install or maintain
Provider secures the infrastructure and platform; the customer manages data and access configuration
The customer's main duties are identity and access management and data classification, not patching servers
SAE: Replaces the WPA2 PSK four-way handshake
Resists offline dictionary attacks, even with a weak passphrase
SAML: XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between an identity provider and a service provider
The IdP issues an assertion that the service provider consumes, so credentials are not re-entered
Lets employees reach many web apps with one corporate identity
SAN: Usually Subject Alternative Name: a certificate field listing extra identities, such as domain names or IP addresses
One certificate can secure multiple domains or subdomains
Modern browsers require a matching SAN entry and increasingly ignore the Common Name alone
Also Storage Area Network: a dedicated high-speed network giving block-level access to consolidated storage
SASE: Cloud-delivered architecture that converges WAN networking with network security
Security functions include CASB, secure web gateway and ZTNA
Gives remote and distributed users secure access without routing back through a central data center
Combines SD-WAN with cloud-native, identity-aware security in one service edge
SCADA: Architecture to monitor and control industrial processes across large geographic areas
Common in utilities, water treatment and manufacturing
Combines remote terminal units, sensors and a central control system
Challenges: legacy protocols and limited patching windows; segment the network, since availability often outweighs confidentiality
SCAP: NIST suite of standards for automated vulnerability management, measurement and compliance checking
Includes component standards such as CVE and OVAL
Lets compatible tools run standardized, repeatable security checks
SCEP: Protocol that automates requesting and issuing certificates for large numbers of devices
Used by MDM and UEM platforms to enroll mobile devices without manual steps
Example: certificates for corporate Wi-Fi or VPN
Cuts PKI administration effort across big device fleets
SCSI: Standards for connecting computers to peripherals such as hard drives and tape drives
Exposed or misconfigured iSCSI targets are a data exposure risk: use authentication and segmentation
SD-WAN: Virtualized management of WAN connections across multiple sites
Routes traffic over the best available path based on application needs
Applies security and routing policy centrally
Improves branch connectivity, replaces costly MPLS links and is a building block of SASE
SDK: Collection of tools, libraries, documentation and code samples for building apps on a platform or service
A vulnerable or malicious SDK brings flaws into every app that embeds it
A supply chain risk, and relevant to secure coding practices
SDLC: Structured process of planning, designing, building, testing, deploying and maintaining software
Security should be built into every phase: DevSecOps, or shifting left
Early security reduces the cost and impact of fixing vulnerabilities found late
Insert code review, static and dynamic testing, and threat modeling within the lifecycle
SDLM: The overall methodology chosen to structure the SDLC, such as waterfall, agile, spiral or RAD
Says where security activities like threat modeling and code review fit
A consistent, enforced methodology builds security in rather than bolting it on after release
A documented methodology is a governance control supporting a secure SDLC
SDN: Architecture separating the control plane (forwarding decisions) from the data plane (forwarding traffic)
Network behavior is managed centrally and programmatically through software
Replaces manual configuration of individual devices
Enables centralized security policy, microsegmentation and automated response
SE Linux: Linux kernel security module that enforces mandatory access control
Restricts what processes and users can do, regardless of standard file permissions
Confines a compromised application to a limited set of allowed actions
A real-world MAC implementation: labels and policies work independently of owner-set permissions
SED: Drive with encryption hardware built into its controller
Automatically encrypts everything written, using a key that never leaves the drive
Full-disk encryption with minimal performance cost and no host software
Protects data at rest even if the drive is removed, provided it is locked and the key is managed securely
SEH: Windows mechanism that manages how a program responds to runtime errors and exceptions
Attackers overwrite handler records during a buffer overflow
The corrupted handler redirects execution to attacker-controlled code when triggered
SFTP: Secure file transfer over an encrypted SSH connection
Gives confidentiality, integrity and strong authentication for transferred files
The encrypted replacement for FTP; not FTPS, which wraps FTP in TLS
SHA: Family of cryptographic hash functions producing a fixed-length digest
Used for integrity, digital signatures and password storage
SHA-1 and MD5 are broken and would be findings in an assessment
SHTTP: Early protocol that secured individual HTTP messages with encryption and digital signatures
Superseded by HTTPS, which secures the whole transport connection with TLS/SSL
A legacy, rarely used protocol; it is not what secures the modern web
SIEM: Platform that aggregates, correlates and analyzes log and event data from across the organization in real time
Detects security incidents and supports investigations
Centralizes visibility that would otherwise be scattered across many device logs
Correlation rules and alerting: scenarios involve spotting an incident through correlated logs from several sources
SIM: Small smart card in a mobile device storing the subscriber's identity, keys and network credentials
Used to connect to a cellular carrier
SIM swapping: tricking a carrier into porting a victim's number to a new SIM
