Used to intercept SMS-based MFA codes, so app or hardware-token MFA is preferred
SLA: Formal contract between a provider and customer with measurable performance commitments
Examples: uptime percentage, response times, remediation timelines
Gives a contractual basis to hold the vendor accountable
Often includes security incident response timeframes
SLE: Money lost in a single occurrence of a specific risk event
SLE = asset value x exposure factor
Feeds ALE: ALE = SLE x ARO
A building block of quantitative risk assessment, used to prioritize risk treatment
SMB: Network file-sharing protocol for reading and writing files and requesting services from servers
Mostly used for Windows file and printer sharing
SMBv1 has well-known vulnerabilities, exploited by WannaCry; disable legacy versions
Keep it on internal networks, never exposed to the internet
SMS: Text messaging service on cellular networks
Often used to deliver one-time passcodes for MFA
Vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception
A weaker MFA method than authenticator apps or hardware tokens
SMTP: Standard protocol for sending and relaying email between mail servers
Plaintext by default, with no built-in verification of the sender
SPF and similar controls are layered on top; SMTPS adds encryption
SMTPS: SMTP over an encrypted TLS/SSL connection
Protects email content and credentials in transit
Submission typically on port 465 or 587 with STARTTLS, versus plain SMTP on port 25
An S on a protocol name generally means a TLS-wrapped version
SNMP: Protocol for monitoring and managing network devices such as routers, switches and servers
Collects status information and allows configuration changes
SNMPv1 and v2c send community strings in cleartext, a weak shared secret
Upgrade to SNMPv3, which adds authentication and encryption
SOAP: XML-based messaging protocol for exchanging structured information between web services
More rigid and verbose than REST and JSON APIs
Has built-in standards for message security and transactional reliability
SOAR: Integrates multiple security tools and orchestrates workflows across a security operations center
Automates repetitive investigation and response through predefined playbooks
Example actions: isolating a host or blocking an IP
Integrates with a SIEM; cuts analyst workload and mean time to respond
SOC: Centralized team and facility that continuously monitors, detects, analyzes and responds to security incidents
Relies on SIEM, EDR and threat intelligence feeds
Works through analyst escalation tiers and workflows
SoC: Single chip combining a processor, memory and other components such as graphics or networking
Found in smartphones, IoT devices and embedded systems
Tight integration makes patching harder, and a flaw in one component can affect the whole device
Not the same as SOC, the Security Operations Center
SOW: Document defining the scope, deliverables, timeline and responsibilities of a project or engagement
Sets the legal boundaries of what testers are authorized to do
Acting outside it, even with good intentions, can create legal liability
SOX: U.S. federal law passed after major corporate accounting scandals
Requires publicly traded companies to keep accurate financial records and internal controls over financial reporting
IT controls matter for data integrity
Told apart from HIPAA (health) and GDPR (privacy) by its focus on financial accuracy and executive accountability
SPF: Email authentication where a domain publishes which mail servers may send on its behalf
Implemented as a DNS TXT record listing authorized sending hosts or IP addresses
Receiving servers check it to help detect spoofed sender addresses
One of the email anti-spoofing controls, with DKIM and DMARC
SPIM: Unsolicited spam sent through instant messaging rather than email
Often delivers phishing links or malware
Users trust chat messages more than email, so it works as social engineering
Specifically instant messaging, not email or SMS
SQL: Standard language for querying, inserting, updating and managing data in relational databases
Improperly sanitized input lets attackers inject SQL statements: SQL injection
Injection can read, modify or delete data the attacker should not reach
Root cause is improper input validation; fix with parameterized queries and prepared statements
SQLi: Attack that inserts malicious SQL into improperly validated input fields
Tricks the database into running unintended commands
Can read, modify or delete data, or bypass authentication
Defenses: parameterized queries (prepared statements) and input validation
SRTP: RTP extension adding encryption, message authentication and replay protection to audio and video streams
Stops eavesdropping while keeping RTP's low latency
Relates to RTP as HTTPS relates to HTTP
SSD: Storage that uses flash memory instead of spinning platters
Faster, but harder to erase securely than an HDD
Wear-leveling means overwrite wiping may miss copies of data, and degaussing does not work
Use full-disk encryption or the drive's built-in secure erase command
SSH: Encrypted protocol for secure command-line access to remote systems
Supports password and public-key authentication; keys are preferred
Also tunnels other protocols, such as SFTP
SSID: Human-readable name a wireless access point broadcasts to identify a Wi-Fi network
Hiding it is weak security through obscurity: passive monitoring still finds it
Rogue APs can spoof a legitimate SSID
Evil twin: a rogue AP broadcasting a legitimate-looking SSID to lure victims
SSL: Predecessor to TLS for securing network communications
Obsolete and insecure, with known vulnerabilities such as POODLE
Still used colloquially, even though modern deployments use TLS
Disable it in favor of TLS 1.2 or 1.3; a server still accepting SSL is a finding
SSO: Log in once and reach multiple independent applications without re-entering credentials
Risk concentration: one compromised credential unlocks everything downstream
Implemented with SAML or OAuth; pair it with strong MFA
STIG: Configuration standard from the U.S. Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA)
Detailed, prescriptive hardening instructions for operating systems, applications and network devices
An authoritative secure-configuration baseline, especially in government and defense
Gives specific, actionable settings rather than general policy; used with SCAP-based compliance scanning
STIX: Standard language and format for representing and sharing cyber threat intelligence
Covers indicators, threat actors and attack patterns
Structured and machine-readable, so organizations exchange threat data consistently
STIX is the format; TAXII is the transport
SWG: Appliance or cloud service that sits between users and the internet
Enforces acceptable use policy and filters malicious or inappropriate content
Inspects web traffic for threats such as malware downloads
Gives central visibility and control of outbound browsing, wherever users connect from
TACACS+: Encrypts the entire authentication packet, unlike RADIUS, which encrypts only the password
Separates authentication, authorization and accounting into distinct processes
Granular control over which commands a user can run on network devices
Uses TCP port 49; common for device administration on routers and switches
TAXII: Application protocol for transporting cyber threat intelligence between organizations and platforms
Makes threat intel feeds shareable and consumable automatically
The transport layer, not the data format
TCP: Connection-oriented transport protocol: a reliable session set up by a three-way handshake
The basis for HTTP, SSH and many others
Handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; the basis for understanding SYN flood attacks
UDP is the connectionless, best-effort contrast
TCP/IP: Foundational protocol suite governing how data is addressed, transmitted, routed and received across the internet
Layered structure that maps loosely to the OSI model
Helps place where firewalls and IDS/IPS operate, and troubleshoot connectivity
Protocols that run on top include HTTP, DNS and FTP
TGT: Credential the KDC issues in Kerberos after a user authenticates
Lets the user request service tickets without re-entering a password
Time-limited, and it reduces how often credentials cross the network
Flow: the KDC's Authentication Service issues the TGT, then the Ticket Granting Service issues service tickets
TKIP: Encryption protocol from the original WPA, an interim fix for WEP
Generates a unique key for each packet
Replaced by AES-CCMP in WPA2 and WPA3; a network still allowing TKIP is a finding
TLS: Modern protocol securing network communication in transit
Gives confidentiality, integrity and server (optionally client) authentication
Successor to SSL; underlies HTTPS and secure email
TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are the recommended versions
The handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to set up a shared symmetric session key
TOC: Moment a program checks a condition, such as a file's permissions or state, before acting
First half of the TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) race condition
The risk is an attacker changing the resource in the gap between check and use
TOTP: Temporary numeric passcode derived from a shared secret and the current time
Typically valid for only 30 to 60 seconds
Used as a second factor through an authenticator app
Works without a connection to the authentication server, because it depends on synchronized time
HOTP is counter-based and stays valid until used
TOU: Moment a program actually uses a resource it checked earlier
Second half of TOCTOU: an attacker swaps the resource in the gap, so the program acts on something other than what it validated
Fix: make check-and-use atomic, or use file handles instead of re-resolving paths
TPM: Dedicated hardware chip on the motherboard that generates, stores and manages cryptographic keys
Can attest to the integrity of the boot process
Underpins full-disk encryption key storage and measured or secure boot
A key sealed in the TPM is unavailable if the boot process is tampered with
TSIG: Uses a shared secret key and HMAC to authenticate DNS messages
Secures dynamic DNS updates and zone transfers between servers
Only a server with the correct key can change a DNS zone
DNSSEC instead authenticates responses to clients using public-key signatures
TTP: Describes a threat actor's behavior patterns: tactics, techniques and procedures
Tactics are high-level strategies, techniques the specific methods, procedures the detailed step-by-step actions
Used to profile adversaries and anticipate their next moves
TTPs: Framework for describing threat actor behavior: tactics, techniques and procedures
Builds from general strategy down to specific implementation
Used for attribution and detection engineering, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
Describes behavior patterns, unlike a single indicator such as an IP address
UAT: Final phase of testing where real end users validate the application against business requirements
Done in realistic scenarios before production release
Should include realistic data handling and permission scenarios, not only functional checks
Sits at the end of the SDLC and change management, just before deployment
UAV: Remotely piloted or autonomous aircraft, a drone
Legitimate uses: facility inspection and perimeter surveillance
Offensive uses: unauthorized surveillance, signal jamming, capturing images of badge codes or screens
Can place a rogue access point within range of a target's Wi-Fi from outside the perimeter
UDP: Connectionless transport protocol: no session setup, no guaranteed delivery, order or error correction
Trades reliability for speed and low overhead
Used by DNS, DHCP and streaming media
No handshake means source IPs can be spoofed, so it suits amplification and reflection DDoS (DNS, NTP)
UEBA: Uses machine learning and statistics to baseline normal user and device behavior
Flags anomalies that may mean compromised credentials or insider threats
Catches subtle attacks that signature-based tools miss, like a legitimate account suddenly accessing unusual resources
Behavioral and anomaly-based detection, often integrated with or feeding a SIEM
UEFI: Modern firmware interface replacing legacy BIOS
Initializes hardware and loads the operating system
Supports Secure Boot, larger drives and a richer pre-boot environment
Secure Boot verifies that only trusted, signed bootloaders and OS components run, stopping bootkits and rootkits
UEM: Single console combining mobile device, application and traditional desktop and laptop management
Enforces consistent security policy across every endpoint type
The evolution of separate MDM and EMM tools
Used to push patches, enforce encryption and remotely wipe lost or stolen devices
UPS: Battery-backed device giving short-term emergency power during an outage
Gives systems time to shut down gracefully or switch to a generator
Supports availability by protecting against abrupt power loss
A short-term bridge, not a replacement for a generator in an extended outage
URI: String that uniquely identifies a resource, such as a web page, file or API endpoint
A URL is the most common type of URI, one that also says how to reach the resource
A URI can just name a resource without saying how to fetch it
Attackers embed malicious or encoded characters for directory traversal or injection
URL: Text address that locates a resource on the internet, giving protocol, domain and path
Attackers disguise URLs in phishing: typosquatting, URL shorteners, homograph look-alike characters
Scenarios ask you to spot a suspicious URL in an email or message
USB: Standard interface for connecting peripherals and storage devices to a computer
Common vector for data exfiltration and malware, such as a dropped infected flash drive
Mitigation: disable or restrict USB mass storage through endpoint policy
DLP and endpoint controls can restrict it
USB OTG: Specification letting a mobile device act as a USB host
Connects directly to flash drives, keyboards or other phones with no computer in between
A data exfiltration risk: a phone can read or write straight to a USB drive, bypassing cloud DLP
Some MDM or UEM policies disable it
UTM: Single appliance consolidating firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus, content filtering and VPN
Simplifies management for smaller organizations compared with separate point solutions
Trade-off: a single point of failure or bottleneck against simple consolidated management
UTP: Common copper network cabling, such as Cat5e or Cat6
Twists wire pairs together to reduce electromagnetic interference, with no extra shielding
Cheap and widely used for standard Ethernet
More prone to interference and eavesdropping than shielded twisted pair or fiber
VBA: Scripting language built into Microsoft Office that automates tasks through macros
Attackers hide malicious macros in Word or Excel documents
The code runs when the victim opens the file and enables macros
A common phishing attachment vector; disable macros by default or allow only signed macros
VDE: Individual virtual desktop session a user interacts with
Runs on a server and is streamed to the user's endpoint
VDI is the overall infrastructure; the VDE is a single user's desktop session
Keeps sensitive data on the server instead of the endpoint and applies consistent controls to every session
VDI: Backend infrastructure that hosts and manages virtual desktops on central servers
Delivers a consistent desktop to thin clients, laptops or tablets
Computing and data stay in the data center, so a lost or stolen endpoint exposes little or nothing
A strong control for BYOD, where endpoints are not fully trusted or managed
VLAN: Logical segmentation of a physical network into separate broadcast domains
Isolates groups of devices without separate switches or cabling
Traffic between VLANs must pass through a router or Layer 3 device
VLAN hopping exploits misconfigured trunk ports
VLSM: Subnetting a network into subnets of different sizes
More efficient use of IP address space than equal-sized blocks
Wastes fewer addresses than fixed-size classful subnetting
Supports network segmentation, a key security control for isolating trust levels
VM: Software emulation of a physical computer, running its own OS on a hypervisor
Gives workload isolation and rapid provisioning
VM escape: an attacker breaks out of a guest to reach the hypervisor or other VMs on the host
Primary defense: keep the hypervisor patched
VoIP: Carries voice calls as digital data over IP networks instead of analog phone lines
Typically RTP for the media and SIP or similar for call signaling
Shares the network with other data, so it needs its own security
Put phones on a separate VLAN and use SRTP to prevent eavesdropping and toll fraud
VPC: Isolated, logically segmented section of a public cloud
Has its own private IP addressing, subnets and network controls
Gives cloud tenants segmentation similar to a traditional private data center
Control subnetting, routing and security groups or ACLs, isolated from other tenants
VPN: Encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet
Lets remote users or sites reach private resources as if directly connected
Protects confidentiality and integrity in transit; can mask the user's IP address and location
Forms: remote access and site-to-site; underlying protocols include IPsec and TLS
Split tunnel sends only some traffic through the VPN; full tunnel sends everything
VTC: Systems that let people in different places talk using real-time video and audio
Unsecured sessions can be joined by uninvited participants (meeting bombing)
Unencrypted streams can be intercepted, exposing sensitive discussions
Controls: meeting passwords, waiting rooms and encryption
WAF: Filters, monitors and blocks malicious HTTP/HTTPS traffic to and from a web application
Defends against attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting
Works at the application layer, inspecting request content rather than only IP addresses and ports
A traditional network firewall filters at lower layers
WAP: Device that lets wireless clients connect to a wired network over Wi-Fi
Misconfigured or rogue WAPs bypass perimeter security
A rogue WAP plugged into a network jack creates a backdoor
Detect and prevent with WIPS and port security
WEP: Early Wi-Fi encryption standard using a weak, static implementation of RC4
Completely broken: crackable in minutes with common tools
Never an acceptable answer for securing a wireless network
WIDS: Monitors the radio spectrum and wireless traffic for threats
Detects unauthorized access points, rogue devices and attacks like deauthentication floods and evil twins
Detection only: it alerts but does not block, unlike WIPS
Sees wireless threats that a wired IDS or IPS would miss
WIPS: Monitors the wireless spectrum and automatically responds to threats
Handles rogue access points, evil twin networks and wireless denial of service
Can take active measures, such as disconnecting unauthorized devices
Same split as IPS vs IDS: WIPS acts, WIDS only alerts
WO: Formal document that authorizes and records a specific task, such as maintenance, a change or a repair
Records what work is needed, who approved it and who performed it
Gives an auditable trail linking approved changes to the technicians who did them
WPA: Wireless security standard introduced to replace the flawed WEP
Used TKIP as an interim fix
Evolution: WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3, each fixing weaknesses in the one before
WPA2: Wireless standard that replaced WPA, using AES-based CCMP encryption
Strong confidentiality and integrity; the dominant standard for over a decade
Personal mode is open to offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake
WPA3: Replaces WPA2's pre-shared key handshake with SAE, resisting offline dictionary attacks even with weak passwords
Adds individualized encryption on open networks through Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE)
The best-practice answer for new wireless deployments
WPS: Feature for connecting devices to Wi-Fi easily with a PIN or a button press
The PIN method is vulnerable to brute force, which can recover the actual passphrase
Recommended to disable on home and enterprise access points
WTLS: Security protocol for the Wireless Application Protocol (WAP) on older, low-power mobile devices
Provided authentication, encryption and data integrity
Largely abandoned: modern smartphones use standard TLS
A legacy protocol, outdated compared with full TLS
XaaS: Umbrella term for any IT capability delivered as a subscription cloud service
Examples: software, infrastructure, platforms, security and storage
Instead of being owned and maintained on premises
A catch-all for models beyond IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, such as security-as-a-service or disaster-recovery-as-a-service
XCCDF: Authors standardized, machine-readable security configuration checklists and benchmarks
Automated tools use them to assess compliance against a baseline
Often paired with OVAL, which describes how to check system state
XDR: Platform that correlates telemetry from endpoints, network, email and cloud in one detection and response system
Goes beyond a single-domain tool like EDR
Broader visibility and more automated cross-layer response than siloed point products
An evolution beyond EDR, which covers endpoints only
XML: Markup language that structures and exchanges data in a human-readable, tag-based format
Used in web services, configuration files and data feeds
Poorly secured parsers allow XML External Entity (XXE) injection
XXE can expose local files or enable server-side request forgery; disable external entity processing
XOR: Logical operation that outputs true only when exactly one of its two inputs is true
Reversible: applying the same key with XOR twice returns the original data
A building block of stream ciphers and the one-time pad
A truly random, single-use key makes it theoretically unbreakable; reusing or shortening the key breaks it
XSRF: Another name for CSRF: cross-site request forgery
Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request to a site where they are authenticated
Performs unwanted actions, such as changing an email address or transferring funds
Exploits the site's trust in the browser session; mitigations: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, checking request origin
Different from XSS, which injects script rather than forging a request
XSS: Web vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious client-side script into pages other users view
The victim's browser runs the script: session cookie theft or defacement
Caused by insufficient input validation and output encoding
Mitigations: input validation or sanitization, output encoding, and a WAF as a compensating control
ZTNA: Grants access to applications and resources through strict, continuous identity verification and least-privilege policy
Never trust, always verify: nothing is trusted just for being inside the perimeter
Replaces the old implicit-trust VPN model
Zero Trust architecture ideas: control plane and data plane, policy enforcement points
